A Visit That Brought Farming Closer

Last Saturday, the Student Union organized a visit to a local farm, giving students an opportunity to understand where their food comes from. Thirty volunteers joined the activity and received a warm welcome from the farmers.

The visit began with a short introduction to seasonal crops. Students then helped plant vegetables and learned how to water young plants without wasting resources. A farmer explained that successful farming requires patience as well as practical knowledge. During the discussion, participants asked questions about food safety and the difficulties faced by small farms.

The activity ended with students sharing their observations. Many said that they would appreciate every meal more and reduce food waste. The Student Union plans to organize similar visits in the future, helping students connect classroom knowledge with everyday life.

Last Sunday, our Student Union organized a visit to a Hope elementary school. Twenty students took part in the event, hoping to support local children and learn more about educational opportunities in rural areas.

The visitors brought storybooks and sports equipment collected on campus. After a brief welcome, they helped the children read simple English stories and played team games together. Teachers thanked the volunteers and discussed the school's need for more reading materials.

Before leaving, the visitors promised to continue supporting the school through a regular book collection. Participants said that the experience reminded them of the importance of equal access to education. This meaningful visit connected university students with children who have different learning conditions.

A Caring Afternoon in Our Neighborhood

The Student Union organized a volunteer activity last Saturday to assist elderly residents in the neighborhood. More than twenty students joined the program, which aimed to offer practical help and strengthen connections between the university and the community.

After receiving basic safety instructions, volunteers worked in small groups. Some cleaned rooms and carried heavy shopping bags, while others showed residents how to make video calls to their families. Students also spent time listening to the residents' stories. These conversations helped them understand that companionship can be as valuable as material support.

At the end of the afternoon, several residents expressed their gratitude and invited the volunteers to return. The Student Union will arrange regular visits rather than treating the activity as a single event. Participants left with a stronger sense of responsibility and a better understanding of caring for others.

I am glad that you want to learn Chinese, and I would recommend Beijing as a place to begin your learning journey. It offers opportunities to combine language classes with everyday practice.

Many universities and language schools provide courses for international learners. You can choose a class that matches your level and gives you enough time to practice speaking. Yours,
Li Ming

The use of translation apps is becoming increasingly popular. These tools help people understand foreign signs, communicate while traveling and get the general meaning of unfamiliar texts. However, convenience should not be confused with complete accuracy.

A translation app can save time when a learner meets a new expression. For example, checking a short instruction may allow someone to finish a practical task without waiting for help. Yet a sentence may contain humor, cultural references or several possible meanings. An automatic translation can miss these details and even change the writer's intention. Students who copy every translated sentence may also lose opportunities to think independently.

Therefore, I believe translation apps should be used as assistants rather than replacements for learning. We can compare their suggestions with examples, consult reliable dictionaries and ask teachers when necessary. Using technology thoughtfully makes communication easier while helping us develop lasting language skills.

The online library is becoming increasingly popular. For students, it opens a convenient door to books and research materials that may otherwise be difficult to obtain. Its value lies not simply in storing information, but in making learning more accessible.

First, an online library allows readers to search for materials without traveling to a particular building. A student preparing a report can compare several articles at home and save useful notes. Second, digital resources can support learners whose schedules prevent them from visiting a library during normal hours. Nevertheless, access alone does not guarantee effective study. Readers must evaluate sources carefully, respect copyright and avoid being distracted by other websites.

In my view, universities should improve digital collections while teaching students how to use them responsibly. Online and physical libraries can support each other. When convenient access is combined with careful reading, the online library becomes a valuable partner in independent learning.

The use of PowerPoint is becoming increasingly popular in class. A well-designed presentation can make a lesson clearer, but its effectiveness depends on how teachers and students use it.

Pictures, charts and short videos can explain ideas that are difficult to express through words alone. In a science lesson, for example, a simple diagram may show the steps of an experiment more clearly than a long paragraph. Slides can also help students review the main points after class. However, putting an entire textbook on the screen often encourages passive copying. If a teacher reads every line without discussion, students may see the information without understanding it.

I therefore support using PowerPoint as one teaching tool among several. Teachers should keep slides concise and leave time for questions, practice and conversation. Students should take meaningful notes rather than copy everything. A successful class needs active thinking, not merely attractive slides.

Online dictionaries are becoming increasingly popular. They make it possible to check a word quickly and hear its pronunciation, even when a printed dictionary is not available. For language learners, this is a useful change.

Their greatest advantage is the variety of information they can provide. Besides a short meaning, learners may find examples, common expressions and notes about how a word is used. When reading an article, I often compare several examples before deciding which meaning fits the sentence. However, quick access can also create careless habits. Choosing the first translation without considering context may lead to misunderstanding, and advertisements may interrupt study.

In my opinion, students should select reliable dictionaries and use them with a clear purpose. We need to read examples, notice grammar and record words worth reviewing. An online dictionary can support independent learning, but understanding still requires our attention and judgment.

The way people receive education has changed greatly. A classroom with a teacher and a blackboard is still important, but learning now also takes place through digital platforms, shared resources and activities beyond school.

One noticeable change is greater flexibility. Students can watch a lesson again when a difficult idea needs more explanation. They can also discuss a project with classmates in different places. Another change is the growing emphasis on participation. Instead of only listening and memorizing, learners are often encouraged to ask questions, solve problems and connect knowledge with real situations. However, these improvements do not benefit everyone equally. Some students lack suitable devices or a quiet place to study.

In my view, better education requires both useful technology and thoughtful support. Schools should help teachers design effective lessons and ensure that students can participate. Whatever the method, education should develop understanding, curiosity and the ability to learn independently.

Are People Becoming Addicted to Technology?

Technology has become part of almost every activity, and some people find it difficult to put their devices away. Although frequent use alone does not prove addiction, losing control over that use deserves attention.

For example, a student may plan to check one message before studying, only to spend an hour watching short videos. If this pattern repeatedly harms sleep, schoolwork or relationships, it is more than a harmless habit. However, technology also enables useful learning and communication, so blaming every device would be unreasonable. The important issue is whether a person can choose when to stop.

We should therefore develop practical boundaries. Turning off unnecessary notifications, setting aside time without screens and seeking support when daily life is seriously affected can help. Technology ought to serve our goals. Recognizing unhealthy patterns early allows us to enjoy its advantages without letting it control our attention.

Is Technology Making People Lazy?

Technology can reduce effort, but whether it makes people lazy depends largely on how they use it. Saving time on a routine task may support deeper work, while avoiding every challenge can weaken independent thinking.

Consider a student who uses a computer to organize research notes. The tool allows more time for comparing ideas and developing an argument. By contrast, another student may copy an answer found online without checking its meaning. The same technology then becomes a shortcut around learning. Constant entertainment and notifications can also make it harder to concentrate on demanding tasks.

I believe the answer is not to reject technology but to use it purposefully. Before opening an application, we should identify the problem we want to solve and decide which thinking we must do ourselves. Useful tools improve our abilities when they support effort. They encourage laziness only when we let them replace that effort.

Do Violent Video Games Lead to Violence?

The relationship between violent video games and real-life behavior deserves careful discussion. Research raising concerns about aggression should be taken seriously, but it does not mean that every player will become violent.

Repeated exposure to aggressive scenes may influence how some children respond to conflict, especially when they lack guidance. At the same time, family relationships, personal experiences and the social environment also shape behavior. It would be too simple to blame one type of entertainment for every incident. Parents and teachers should therefore pay attention to a child's overall habits instead of judging by a game alone.

In my opinion, age-appropriate choices and reasonable time limits are important. Adults can discuss the difference between fictional action and acceptable behavior, encourage cooperative activities and notice worrying changes early. A balanced approach protects children while avoiding unsupported claims. The goal should be responsible entertainment and healthy relationships, not a careless argument about games.

A Report on Our Used-Book Collection

Our university completed a used-book collection project last week to reduce waste and share learning resources. Organized by the Student Union with support from the library, the project attracted students from several departments.

Volunteers placed collection boxes in residence halls and explained which books could be donated. They checked the condition of each book, sorted donations by subject and recorded basic information. Books suitable for further study were made available at a campus exchange corner, while children's storybooks were prepared for donation to a community reading room. Damaged books were sent for responsible recycling.

As a participant, I learned that a successful collection requires more than gathering a large number of items. Careful sorting and clear arrangements help books reach readers who need them. The organizers plan to repeat the project next term and improve publicity based on the volunteers' suggestions.

A Proposal to Improve Library Services

I would like to suggest several improvements to our school library. Although its collections are valuable, crowded study areas and difficulties locating materials sometimes prevent students from using them effectively.

First, students often spend time searching for a seat during examination weeks. The library could introduce a simple booking system and release seats that remain unused for a reasonable period. Second, some readers find the catalogue difficult to navigate. Short training sessions and clear signs near the entrance would help them identify useful resources. A regular suggestion form could also allow students to recommend books related to their courses.

These changes should be tested on a small scale before wider introduction. Library staff and student representatives could review feedback together and adjust the arrangements. By improving access to both space and information, the library would become a more welcoming place for focused study and independent research.

A Proposal for Richer Extracurricular Activities

I suggest that our Student Union develop a balanced program of extracurricular activities. Students need opportunities to exercise, explore interests and contribute to the community, rather than attend only large performances.

A weekly sports session could welcome beginners and offer different levels of participation. This would help students stay active without feeling pressured to compete. Finally, monthly volunteer visits could connect students with nearby communities and encourage a sense of responsibility.

To make the program accessible, most activities should be free or inexpensive and scheduled around major examinations. Organizers could collect suggestions through a short survey before deciding the timetable. Providing varied choices would help students find meaningful ways to spend their free time, make friends and develop abilities that ordinary classroom lessons may not cover.

Our class celebrated Teachers' Day last Friday with a series of activities to express gratitude to the teachers who guide our studies. Class representatives organized the event, and every student was invited to contribute.

The celebration brought our class closer and reminded us that gratitude should continue beyond a single special day.

A distinguished scholar delivered a lecture on independent learning at our university yesterday. The talk emphasized that university education should help students develop the ability to ask useful questions, not simply remember information.

The speaker first encouraged students to connect classroom ideas with problems in everyday life. He explained that a small observation can become the beginning of a meaningful investigation. Next, he discussed the importance of evaluating evidence. Students should compare sources, recognize uncertainty and be willing to revise their conclusions. Finally, he recommended cooperation, noting that a discussion with people from different subjects can reveal assumptions we have overlooked.

The lecture attracted thoughtful questions from the audience. Its central message was that curiosity needs disciplined effort to become real understanding. Students left with practical suggestions for reading, discussion and research that could be applied to their current studies.

What impresses me most about my university is the atmosphere of shared learning in its library. The building is useful, but the people and habits within it make the place special to me.

When I first arrived, I struggled to find materials for a course project. A student volunteer showed me how to search the catalogue and compare different sources. Later, I noticed that classmates often exchanged reading suggestions while respecting the quiet study areas. Staff also offered short introductions to research resources, making unfamiliar tools less intimidating. These small forms of support encouraged me to ask better questions and study more independently.

The library represents a wider quality that I value in the university: knowledge is something to explore together rather than keep to oneself. I hope to contribute by helping new students as others helped me. This everyday spirit of cooperation has left a deeper impression than any single ceremony.

Public access, however, needs clear arrangements. During examination weeks, students often struggle to find seats. The library could therefore reserve study areas for students and admit outside visitors mainly during quieter periods. Visitors should register before entering and follow the same rules about noise and book care as everyone else. Such measures would make the policy fairer and easier to manage.

The university could begin with weekend access to selected reading rooms. Staff should collect feedback from both students and visitors before expanding the service. With suitable hours, reasonable visitor limits and enough staff support, an open library can serve the public while fulfilling its central responsibility to students.

I support opening university sports facilities to the public during suitable hours. These spaces could give local residents more opportunities to exercise and encourage friendly exchanges between the university and its neighbors.

Students' regular classes and training should receive priority. A booking system could show which courts are available to visitors after teaching activities have been arranged. The university should also set reasonable visitor limits, publish safety rules and provide basic staff supervision. These steps would reduce crowding and help everyone use the facilities responsibly.

After several weeks, the university could review costs, safety records and student feedback. Public access would then develop according to actual capacity. A carefully organized policy can benefit the community without weakening the university's teaching services.

I believe College Chinese should be a compulsory course if its teaching is relevant to university students. The course can strengthen our ability to understand complex texts, express ideas clearly and appreciate the culture behind the language.

These skills matter in every discipline. A science student must explain a project accurately, while a business student needs to write a convincing report. Reading selected literary works can also encourage reflection on human experience and different ways of thinking. Therefore, the course should go beyond repeating material already covered in secondary school.

Practical teaching would make the requirement worthwhile. Students could discuss short texts, revise their own writing and connect readings with their fields of study. Assessments should value careful reasoning and clear expression rather than mechanical memorization. With suitable content and manageable workloads, a compulsory College Chinese course would provide useful training and a shared opportunity for cultural learning.

AI technology can support learning when students use it with clear purposes and independent judgment. It can explain unfamiliar concepts, suggest practice questions and give feedback, but students remain responsible for understanding the material.

A useful method is to attempt a task before asking AI for help. For example, after solving a mathematics problem, a student can compare the reasoning with an AI explanation and investigate any disagreement. In writing, suggestions may help identify unclear sentences, but the student should choose revisions and check facts against reliable sources. These steps turn assistance into an opportunity to learn.

Universities should explain when AI use is permitted and how it should be acknowledged. Students also need practice recognizing inaccurate answers. If we simply submit generated work, we lose the thinking that education requires. Used thoughtfully, AI can make study more efficient while helping us develop our own abilities.

Cross-cultural communication abilities are essential for students who study and work in an increasingly connected world. Communicating successfully requires more than fluent language; it also involves understanding different expectations and showing respect.

Students can begin by learning how everyday behavior varies across cultures. For example, ways of giving feedback or expressing disagreement may differ. We should ask polite questions instead of judging unfamiliar behavior too quickly. Joint projects with international classmates offer opportunities to practice this habit. Listening carefully and checking that everyone understands a task can prevent unnecessary misunderstandings.

Universities could support these efforts through discussion groups, exchange activities and courses that use realistic situations. After each activity, students should reflect on what worked and what caused confusion. We do not need to memorize a fixed description of every culture. By remaining curious, flexible and respectful, we can build relationships and cooperate effectively with people from different backgrounds.

I agree that all university students should learn the basics of academic writing. Regardless of their major, students need to organize ideas, evaluate evidence and explain conclusions clearly. These abilities are useful both in coursework and in future employment.

A suitable course should teach students how to develop a question, build a logical argument and acknowledge sources. For example, a short report can require students to compare two reliable articles and explain why they support a particular conclusion. Revising this report after feedback would be more valuable than memorizing complicated expressions.

However, the requirement should allow for differences between disciplines. An engineering report and a literature essay may use different structures, although both need clear reasoning and honest use of evidence. Universities could offer shared introductory lessons followed by subject-related practice. With manageable assignments and helpful feedback, required academic writing training would strengthen students' thinking as well as their communication.

Students can make better use of campus resources by connecting them with clear academic goals. A library, laboratory or consultation service becomes valuable when we know what we need and take the initiative to ask for support.

First, students should learn what resources are available. Library workshops can teach us to find reliable research materials, while office hours provide opportunities to discuss difficult concepts with teachers. We should prepare specific questions before seeking help, rather than expecting someone else to complete our work. Second, study groups can turn individual resources into shared learning opportunities. Explaining an idea to a classmate often reveals gaps in our own understanding.

Practical planning is also essential. Students can set a weekly goal, choose the resources needed and review their progress. Booking facilities responsibly ensures that others can benefit too. Through purposeful use and consistent effort, campus resources can support deeper learning and independent academic development.

I support requiring university students to participate in at least one research project, provided that the projects match their abilities and available resources. Research can teach students to ask meaningful questions, examine evidence and revise ideas when results challenge their expectations.

Its value does not depend on making a major discovery. A small survey or a carefully designed experiment can help students understand how knowledge is produced. Working with classmates also develops planning and communication skills. These experiences connect classroom learning with real investigation.

Practical arrangements are essential, however. Universities should provide introductory training, clear supervision and projects of different sizes. Students from different majors need suitable options, and heavy costs should not prevent participation. Assessment should focus on honest methods and thoughtful reflection rather than impressive findings. With a manageable timetable and sufficient guidance, the requirement can be both necessary for intellectual development and practical to carry out.

Robots may play a useful role in future campus life if their applications address clear needs. Rather than introducing machines simply for novelty, universities should choose tasks where robots can provide reliable help.

For example, delivery robots could carry books or equipment between campus buildings. Cleaning robots might support staff in large public areas, while laboratory robots could help students observe precise experimental procedures. These uses would save time and create opportunities to learn about technology. However, machines must be tested carefully so that they do not block paths or create risks for pedestrians.

Universities should also explain how personal information is handled and provide human support when a robot fails. Students and staff could give feedback during small trials before wider use. Robots would be most valuable as well-managed tools within existing services. Their future on campus should depend on practical benefits, accessibility and safety rather than impressive demonstrations alone.

I propose that our university improve daily services through clearer information and simpler access. Students often lose time searching for opening hours, reporting maintenance problems or finding the right office. A coordinated approach could make campus life easier.

First, the university should provide one regularly updated page for essential information, including clinic hours, transport schedules and contact details. Notices should use clear language and be easy to read on mobile phones. Second, a straightforward system for reporting broken facilities could show whether a request has been received and when it is expected to be handled.

The university should consult students before introducing these changes. A short trial in several buildings would reveal practical problems, while staff feedback would help set realistic response times. Students also need an accessible way to ask for human help. By improving information and everyday service procedures, the university can reduce frustration and leave students more time for learning and rest.
